subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 19 periods = 760 minutes
Total: 19 periods · 12h 40min

periods.activity_title: Discovering the Circle Through Compass Exploration

textbook_items_in_class.description: Students mark a point P, then use a compass set to 4 cm to trace all points 4 cm from P, discovering that the resulting curve is a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: What radius should be taken in the compass to draw the first half-circle of the Wavy Wave? What should be the length of AX?

time_bands.activity: Students attempt to replicate the wave and eyes figures freehand, then compare the results with a neighbour, noticing which curves are difficult to reproduce accurately without a tool.

Activity (compass exploration), section 8.1 p.188 ("students mark point P; use compass set to 4 cm to trace all points….") — each student sets a compass to 4 cm, anchors it on a marked centre P, and rotates it to trace the full curve, arriving at the definition of a circle: every point on the curve is exactly 4 cm from P.

Construct (Wavy Wave), section 8.1 p.191 ("construct a wavy wave on baseline AB of 8 cm by drawing successive half-circles….") — students draw a baseline, locate the midpoint, and swing the first half-circle below, then continue the wave by repositioning the compass centre for each arc.

Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191 ("what radius should be taken to draw the first half-circle of the Wavy Wave?….") — students record the radius and AX length they used, then compare with peers to verify consistency.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who open the compass to the full baseline length rather than half of it; the key insight is that the radius equals half the wave's width. If students struggle with the compass slipping, suggest pressing the compass needle firmly into a cork mat or a thick page.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a wavy wave on a baseline AB of 8 cm by drawing successive half-circles: first half-circle has radius 2 cm centred at the midpoint X of AX = 4 cm, with each subsequent wave mirroring the first.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave on it.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half-circle (as in the neck of 'A Person'). The challenge is to get both waves identical.

time_bands.activity: Construct (Wavy Wave), section 8.1 p.191 ("construct a wavy wave on baseline AB of 8 cm….") — students who need consolidation finish or refine their wave from the previous exploration; students who are ready extend with Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191 ("take a central baseline of a different length…."), choosing a new baseline length and constructing a new wave.

Students attempt the 'A Person' composite figure: they plan the circles (head), arcs (neck wave), and straight lines (body) by estimating suitable radii and centre positions on rough paper first, then execute on clean paper with ruler and compass.

Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191 ("try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half-circle….") — students experiment with compass placement to produce arcs that are less than semicircles, pairing up to compare whether both waves are identical and adjusting centre positions as needed.

periods.teacher_notes: The common error here is placing compass centres by eye rather than by measuring equal distances along the baseline; encourage students to mark the centre points with a pencil dot before drawing the arc. The 'eyes' figure in the textbook is a useful self-check: if the two arcs form a lens shape that is symmetric, the compass placements were equidistant from the central axis.

periods.activity_title: Naming, Rotating, and Verifying Squares and Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (naming square), section 8.2 p.193
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify which of the four given names (PQSR, SPQR, RSPQ, QRSP) is not a valid name for the given square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.2 p.194
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify if any of the four given figures (A, B, C, D) are squares using measurements; then reason whether sides and angles can be determined from dot-grid position alone.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.2 p.194
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid with corners on dots; verify they satisfy the respective properties.

time_bands.activity: Class reads the rectangle naming conventions and the two rectangle properties (opposite sides equal; all angles 90°) and the two square properties (all sides equal; all angles 90°) from section 8.2, then students label a drawn rectangle ABCD identifying corners, opposite sides, and angles.

Figure it Out Q (naming square), section 8.2 p.193 ("identify which of the four given names is not a valid name for the given square….") — students trace the order of corners in each name on the figure and mark valid traversals, then share their reasoning with a partner.

Figure it Out Q2, section 8.2 p.194 ("identify if any of the four given figures are squares using measurements….") — students measure sides and angles of each figure on dot paper and decide which are squares, then reflect on whether dot-grid position alone is sufficient to judge.

Figure it Out Q3, section 8.2 p.194 ("draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid….") — students draw rotated figures with corners on grid dots, measure to verify all required properties hold, and label one figure with a valid name.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent confusion is believing that a tilted square becomes a different shape; reinforce that rotating does not alter side lengths or angles. Watch for students who name corners in a non-traversal order (e.g., PQSR skips around the figure): the valid-name rule requires consecutive corners to be adjacent on the figure.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.2 p.194
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw the rectangle-and-four-squares configuration on dot paper and describe what was done to place the four squares symmetrically around the rectangle.

time_bands.activity: Students study the textbook's rectangle-and-four-squares configuration image and plan their own version on dot paper: they first choose a central rectangle size (in whole dot-units), then identify where the four squares must be placed to sit symmetrically on each side.

Figure it Out Q1, section 8.2 p.194 ("draw the rectangle-and-four-squares configuration on dot paper….") — students execute the full figure, verifying with a ruler that the squares are equal and that each shares exactly one side with the rectangle.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks describing the placement rule they used (e.g., 'each square shares a side of the rectangle and its side length equals the shorter or longer side of the rectangle'), then pairs swap notebooks to check if the description is precise enough to reproduce the figure.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students will attach squares of the wrong size (using the wrong rectangle side as the square's side); the productive error to highlight is that only figures with all four sides equal and all angles 90° qualify as squares attached to the rectangle. The self-check of measuring all four attached squares and comparing is a good habit to name explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Step-by-Step Construction of a Square with Compass and Ruler

textbook_items_in_class.description: Six-step construction of square PQRS with side 6 cm: draw PQ; raise perpendicular at P; mark S at 6 cm on perpendicular; raise perpendicular at Q; use compass to mark R at 6 cm from both S and Q; join to complete.
Draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

time_bands.activity: Class recalls the two square properties (all sides equal; all angles 90°) and identifies which steps in a construction must guarantee each property — a brief oral discussion to motivate the step-by-step procedure.

Construct (Square PQRS, 6 cm), section 8.3 p.195 ("six-step construction of square PQRS with side 6 cm: draw PQ; raise perpendicular at P….") — teacher models each step at the board while students execute simultaneously; after marking R, students measure RS and all four angles to verify the square properties are satisfied.

Construct Q1, section 8.3 p.197 ("draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties….") — students independently apply the same perpendicular-raising technique with adjusted side lengths, measuring opposite sides and all angles after completion to confirm R1 and R2.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is raising the perpendicular by eye rather than by compass arcs; insist that students show the arc marks used to locate the perpendicular, as these are evidence of method. Students who finish early can be directed to Construct Q2, section 8.3 p.197, the 2 cm × 10 cm rectangle, which tests whether the technique generalises to a highly elongated rectangle.

periods.activity_title: Constructing Rectangles and Investigating Angle Constraints

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.
Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all angles are 90° but opposite sides are not equal? Reason and answer.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q2, section 8.3 p.197 ("draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties….") — students construct the narrow rectangle, encountering the challenge that the longer sides must remain exactly parallel; they verify by measuring both pairs of opposite sides and all four angles.

Try This Q3, section 8.3 p.197 ("is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all angles are 90° but opposite sides are not equal?….") — students attempt a sketch, then reason: if all four angles are 90°, the angle sum is 360°, which is consistent, but students try to close the figure and discover that equal opposite sides are forced.

Pairs share their reasoning for Q3 with the class; the teacher collects the key argument — that drawing three 90° turns forces the fourth side to match the opposite side — and class agrees on a written justification in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: For the 2 cm × 10 cm rectangle, watch for students whose longer sides diverge because the perpendicular at Q was not precisely raised; this is a good moment to re-examine the perpendicular construction arcs. The reasoning question (Q3) often produces the misconception that 90° angles alone determine the shape without a side constraint — guiding students to try a physical construction attempt is more convincing than a verbal argument alone.

periods.activity_title: Closest and Farthest: The Moving-Point Investigation

textbook_items_in_class.description: In rectangle ABCD (AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm), predict and verify by measurement: at which positions of X on AD and Y on BC are they closest and farthest apart?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (table), section 8.4 p.198
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a table recording the length XY for at least three different positions of X and Y (given distances from A and B respectively).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively; observe the resulting length XY and the shape of ABYX.

time_bands.activity: Students construct rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, then mark a point X on AD and a point Y on BC, measuring XY for their chosen positions — a quick individual trial before the structured investigation.

Math Talk, section 8.4 p.198 ("in rectangle ABCD, predict and verify: at which positions of X and Y are they closest and farthest apart?….") — small groups of three predict first (writing a sentence), then measure XY at several positions and report back, building towards a class conjecture.

Figure it Out Q (table), section 8.4 p.198 ("fill a table recording XY for at least three different positions of X and Y….") — students complete the table systematically, then examine whether the minimum XY corresponds to X and Y being directly across from each other (equidistant from A and B).

Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively….") — students fill the equal-distance rows of the table and identify that XY equals AB and ABYX forms a rectangle in these cases, recording the observation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse 'equidistant from A and B' with 'at the midpoint'; make clear that X equidistant from A and B means AX = BY, not that X is at the midpoint of AD. The productive insight — that ABYX becomes a rectangle exactly when AX = BY — is the key claim students should articulate in their own words before moving to the construction work.

periods.activity_title: Farthest Distance, Diagonals, and Compass Length Transfer

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC or BD?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — two squares), section 8.4 p.200
textbook_items_in_class.description: Plan and construct a rectangle divisible into two identical squares: set AF to any chosen length, transfer AF using compass to mark B at AB = AF, raise perpendicular at B, mark C at BC = AF, join to complete rectangle ACDF.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("how does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC?….") — students measure the diagonal of their rectangle from the previous construction, compare it to the maximum XY they recorded in their table, and discuss in pairs whether these are equal and why.

Construct (Breaking Rectangles — two squares), section 8.4 p.200 ("plan and construct a rectangle divisible into two identical squares: set AF to any chosen length, transfer AF using compass….") — teacher demonstrates the compass length-transfer technique (opening the compass to span a segment and swinging an arc to reproduce that length), then students execute the full construction for a length of their choice.

Students verify their rectangle by drawing the internal dividing line and measuring the two resulting squares, confirming all sides are equal and all angles are 90°; they annotate the figure with measurements and write a one-sentence description of how the compass transfer technique avoids measurement error.

periods.teacher_notes: The compass length-transfer step is new and error-prone: students often reset the compass after spanning the segment, losing the exact opening. Remind them to move the compass as a unit — do not change the opening between spanning and swinging. The insight that the diagonal equals the farthest XY distance connects the exploration to the upcoming diagonal investigation in section 8.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares.
Construct a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (sides not divisible), section 8.4 p.201
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give the side lengths of a rectangle that cannot be divided into (a) two identical squares; (b) three identical squares.

time_bands.activity: Students plan on rough paper: to divide a rectangle into three identical squares, what must be the ratio of length to breadth? They write down the ratio (3:1) before constructing.

Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199 ("construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares….") — students choose a square-side length, use the compass transfer technique three times to mark the length along the long side, then raise perpendiculars to complete the rectangle, verifying by drawing and measuring the three internal squares.

Explore (two squares), section 8.4 p.199 ("construct a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares….") — students repeat the process for a 2:1 rectangle, this time choosing a different square-side length to confirm the technique is general.

Figure it Out (sides not divisible), section 8.4 p.201 ("give the side lengths of a rectangle that cannot be divided into (a) two identical squares; (b) three identical squares….") — students reason about divisibility and write examples with justification (e.g., a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle cannot be divided into two identical squares because 5 ÷ 3 is not 2).

periods.teacher_notes: Students who confuse 'three identical squares' with 'three squares of any size' will place the dividing lines unevenly; ask them to measure all three resulting regions before claiming success. The divisibility reasoning in E-17 anticipates the more complex construction challenges ahead and is worth discussing as a class to surface the general principle.

periods.activity_title: Composite Construction Challenges: Square Within and Falling Squares

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it such that the centre of the square coincides with the centre of the rectangle.
Construct three aligned falling squares of side 4 cm each, then replicate the pattern with squares of sides 3 cm, 5 cm, and 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Students sketch a rough plan for each challenge before touching compass or ruler: for the Square within a Rectangle, they mark where the square's corners must lie relative to the 8 cm × 4 cm rectangle's centre.

Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201 ("construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it….") — students first construct the outer rectangle, then find its centre by drawing both diagonals, and finally construct the inner square (side 4 cm) centred on that intersection point.

Construct Q2 (Falling Squares), section 8.4 p.202 ("construct three aligned falling squares of side 4 cm each….") — students plan how the squares share a corner and are aligned diagonally, construct the first square, then locate the next square's corner at the previous square's opposite corner, repeating; they then start the pattern with 3 cm squares.

periods.teacher_notes: Finding the rectangle's centre by intersecting diagonals is the key step for Q1; students who measure to the midpoint of each side and mark it separately often introduce measurement error. For Falling Squares, the cascade alignment depends on placing each new square's corner exactly at the previous square's corner — the compass is more reliable than measuring afresh for each step.

periods.activity_title: Shadings, Holes, and Curves: Creative Construction Challenges

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a shading figure (a square containing smaller squares) with measurements of own choice.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q4 (Square with a Hole), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square with a circular hole at its centre; the hole's centre coincides with the square's centre.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q5 (Square with More Holes), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square with multiple circular holes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side; determine the correct centre placement for the compass to produce symmetric arcs.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q3 (Shadings), section 8.4 p.202 ("construct a shading figure — a square containing smaller squares — with measurements of own choice….") — students plan a nesting of squares (outer side, inner side, gap) on rough paper first, ensuring the inner square fits, then construct and shade alternate regions.

Construct Q4 (Square with a Hole), section 8.4 p.202 ("construct a square with a circular hole at its centre….") — students find the centre by intersecting diagonals, choose a radius smaller than half the side length, and use the compass to draw the circle; Construct Q5 (Square with More Holes), section 8.4 p.202, extends the figure by adding two or three smaller circles at other symmetric positions.

Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202 ("construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side….") — students experiment with different centre positions for each arc (midpoint of each side, corners, etc.) and discuss with a partner which placement produces arcs of equal bulge on all four sides.

periods.teacher_notes: For Square with Curves, the typical error is placing the compass centre at a corner rather than outside the square's side; lead students to discover that the arc centre must lie on the perpendicular bisector of each side at some distance from the midpoint. The open-ended nature of Shadings and Multiple Holes makes this unit well-suited to display work — completed figures can be pinned to the board for a brief gallery moment.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Measuring and Predicting: The Equal Diagonals Discovery

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Explore (diagonal bisects angles equally), section 8.5 p.204
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how the rectangle must be constructed so that its diagonal divides the opposite angles into two equal parts.
Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold.

time_bands.activity: Students draw two rectangles of different dimensions, draw both diagonals in each, and predict (before measuring): are the diagonals equal in length? They write their prediction in one sentence.

Students measure both diagonals of each rectangle with a ruler, record in a table (rectangle dimensions, diagonal 1, diagonal 2), and discover that the diagonals are equal; they label the eight angle fragments a–h as described in section 8.5 and measure each.

Explore (diagonal bisects angles equally), section 8.5 p.204 ("determine how the rectangle must be constructed so that its diagonal divides opposite angles into two equal parts….") — students identify, from their angle measurements, which rectangles produce equal halves (those where the rectangle is actually a square) and articulate the condition.

Math Talk (general laws), section 8.5 p.204 ("frame general laws about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold….") — small groups draft a 'law' statement for each pattern observed, then one group reads aloud and the class evaluates whether the statement is precise and always true.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently assume the two diagonals of any quadrilateral are equal; frame this as a question to test rather than a given, so the measurement result carries more meaning. The identification that equal angle-halves require a square (not any rectangle) is the central reasoning payoff of this exploration — resist confirming it before students have found it themselves.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Constructing Rectangles from Diagonal and Angle Constraints

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Rectangle with diagonal dividing angles 60°/30°), section 8.5 p.205
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle ABCD where diagonal AC divides angle A into 60° and 30°: draw AB, raise a 60° line from B to locate C, draw perpendicular through A, use compass or perpendicular from C to locate D, join to complete the rectangle.
Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°.
Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 45° and 45°; observe what this implies about the sides.

time_bands.activity: Construct (Rectangle with diagonal dividing angles 60°/30°), section 8.5 p.205 ("construct a rectangle ABCD where diagonal AC divides angle A into 60° and 30°….") — teacher leads the class step-by-step: draw AB, use a protractor to draw a 60° line from A, determine where C lies, then raise perpendiculars to complete ABCD; students construct simultaneously.

Construct Q1, section 8.5 p.211 ("construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°….") — students apply the same technique independently, checking that 50° + 40° = 90° (a necessary condition) before beginning.

Construct Q2, section 8.5 p.211 ("construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 45° and 45°; observe what this implies about the sides….") — after constructing, students measure the two sides of the resulting rectangle and observe they are equal, identifying the figure as a square, and write a one-sentence explanation.

periods.teacher_notes: The prerequisite for these constructions is that the two angle portions sum to 90° (the right angle of the rectangle's corner); students who use 50° and 50° will try to construct an impossible figure and should be guided to check the sum first. Watch for students who conflate 'divides angle A' with 'the diagonal makes 60° with the horizontal' — the angle is measured inside the rectangle's corner.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Rectangles Specified by One Side and a Diagonal

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Rectangle, side 5 cm, diagonal 7 cm), section 8.5 p.208
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle with one side CD = 5 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm: draw CD; raise perpendicular at C; draw circle of radius 7 cm centred at D; intersection with the perpendicular gives B; complete the rectangle.
Construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm.
Construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Construct (Rectangle, side 5 cm, diagonal 7 cm), section 8.5 p.208 ("construct a rectangle with one side CD = 5 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm: draw CD; raise perpendicular at C; draw circle of radius 7 cm centred at D….") — teacher models the technique; students construct simultaneously and mark the intersection point B.

Construct Q3, section 8.5 p.211 ("construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm….") — students apply the technique independently; after finding B, they complete the rectangle and measure both diagonals to confirm they are equal.

Construct Q4, section 8.5 p.211 ("construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm….") — students work independently; they also note the length of the second side found and discuss: could they have constructed this rectangle without the diagonal constraint, using just two sides?

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight is that the perpendicular at one end of the known side, combined with an arc of the known diagonal length from the other end, uniquely determines the adjacent corner. A common error is drawing the diagonal arc from the wrong endpoint — encourage students to label the endpoints before beginning. Students who finish early can explore whether any pair (side, diagonal) works, or whether the diagonal must be longer than the side.

textbook_segments.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

periods.activity_title: Locating the Apex: Two Circles, One Point

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a 'House' figure with all border lines 5 cm: draw base and walls; draw arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C; intersection gives apex A equidistant from both; draw arc of radius 5 cm from A to complete the curved roof.
Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Class discusses the House problem: the apex A must be exactly 5 cm from both B and C. Students sketch a rough figure and write down what geometric object contains all points 5 cm from B (a circle of radius 5 cm centred at B), then all points 5 cm from C.

Construct (House, sides 5 cm), section 8.6 p.211 ("construct a House figure with all border lines 5 cm: draw base and walls; draw arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C; intersection gives apex A….") — teacher demonstrates drawing both full circles first to show the two intersections, then introduces Method 2 (arcs only); students construct the house using arcs.

Construct Q1, section 8.6 p.215 ("construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm….") — students independently scale up the construction, then check by measuring all five boundary segments (base, two walls, two roof sides) to confirm each is 7 cm.

periods.teacher_notes: The crucial conceptual step is understanding that the intersection of two circles (or arcs) is the ONLY point satisfying both distance conditions simultaneously; ask students to explain in their own words why a point on only one circle is not sufficient. Watch for students who draw the two arcs with different radii — both arcs must use the same radius equal to the required side length.

textbook_segments.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

periods.activity_title: Equidistant Points in Artwork and the Rhombus Investigation

textbook_items_in_class.description: Recreate 'A Person', 'Wavy Wave', and 'Eyes' from section 8.1 using ideas from the House construction (equidistant-point technique).
Is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it using the arc-intersection technique.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q2, section 8.6 p.215 ("recreate 'A Person', 'Wavy Wave', and 'Eyes' from section 8.1 using the equidistant-point technique….") — students identify, for each artwork figure, where an equidistant-point construction is needed (e.g., locating the top of the head circle so it is equidistant from two reference points) and apply the arc-intersection method to those elements.

Construct Q3, section 8.6 p.215 ("is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it….") — students first reason whether such a figure is possible (yes: a rhombus, where opposite angles need not be 90°) and sketch a rough plan.

Students execute the rhombus construction using arc-intersection: fix one side AB, draw arcs of the same length from A and B to locate vertices D and C respectively; the constraint that AC = AB = CD = DB is enforced by the equal-radius arcs; students measure all four sides and all four angles to confirm the figure is not a square.

periods.teacher_notes: For the artwork recreation, students need not re-derive every circle in the figures — the focus is on identifying at least one place per figure where the equidistant-point technique adds precision over pure estimation. For the rhombus, the common error is treating 'all sides equal' as synonymous with 'square'; the construction itself, which can produce non-right angles, is the most convincing demonstration that a square is a special case.

periods.activity_title: Consolidation: Compass Fluency and Construction Accuracy

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half-circle (as in the neck of 'A Person'). The challenge is to get both waves identical.
Draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191 ("try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half-circle….") — students who have not yet achieved identical waves revisit the challenge, this time marking the centre of each arc explicitly before drawing, to discipline the estimation process.

Construct Q1, section 8.3 p.197 ("draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties….") — students re-execute the construction focusing on clean perpendicular arcs, then annotate the figure with all measurements confirming both properties (R1: opposite sides equal; R2: all angles 90°).

Students choose one of the figures from section 8.2's rotated squares and rectangles and re-draw it on plain (not dot) paper using only compass and ruler, verifying that the result satisfies the required properties; they write a brief reflection identifying which construction step is hardest and how they addressed it.

periods.teacher_notes: This consolidation unit revisits the core instrument-use skills — circle-and-radius understanding, valid naming, perpendicular construction — that underpin all the later sections. Focus attention on students who still rely on the protractor to make 90° rather than using the compass perpendicular method, as later constructions depend on the compass technique.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Consolidation: Reasoning About Rectangle and Diagonal Properties

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC or BD?
Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("how does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC?….") — students who have not completed this revisit it by constructing a fresh rectangle, measuring the diagonal and the maximum XY, and writing a one-sentence conclusion.

Math Talk (general laws), section 8.5 p.204 ("frame general laws about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold….") — students compile the laws they observed across rectangles (diagonals are equal; the diagonal of a square bisects the right angles) into a summary table, then attempt to articulate a deductive argument for one law using only the properties of rectangles and squares.

Pairs exchange their written law statements and test each other's: one partner proposes a rectangle with given dimensions and the other checks whether the stated law correctly predicts the diagonal length or angle split, refining any imprecise phrasing.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive argument asked for in the middle band need not be formal proof — a chain of reasoning ('because all angles in a rectangle are 90°, and the diagonal creates two triangles …') is appropriate for this stage. Common imprecision is stating a law only for a specific measured case; guide students to use quantifier language ('for any rectangle …') to lift the statement to generality.

Construct Q3, section 8.6 p.215 ("is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square?….") — students complete or refine their rhombus construction from the earlier unit, verifying all four sides are equal by compass span, measuring all four angles, and confirming at least one angle is not 90°.

Students write a brief construction journal entry (five to seven sentences) describing the equidistant-point principle in their own words: what a 'point equidistant from two given points' means, how two arcs locate it, and one figure from the chapter where the technique was used; they share with a partner and suggest any clarification.

periods.teacher_notes: The journal entry in the final band serves as both consolidation and self-assessment; look for students who confuse 'equidistant from two points' with 'midpoint of the segment joining them' — the rhombus construction, where A is equidistant from B and D but not at their midpoint, is the best counter-example to offer. Connecting this principle to the definition of a circle (every point on the circle is equidistant from the centre) ties the chapter's opening idea to its closing one.

items.prompt: A square has corners labelled P, Q, R, and S going around it in order. Which of the following is NOT a valid name for this square?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: PQSR is not a valid name because the corners are not listed in the order of travel around the figure — it skips from Q directly to S, bypassing R.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that each successive letter names an adjacent corner when tracing around the square in one direction.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confused about what makes a name invalid; PQRS lists corners in correct traversal order and is valid.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may not recognise that a valid name can start at any corner; QRSP starts at Q and traces in order, making it valid.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have miscounted the traversal; RSPQ starts at R and traces in correct order, making it valid.

inclusivity.support: Trace each name on a drawn square with a finger to check whether consecutive letters are adjacent corners.
inclusivity.challenge: Write two more valid names and one more invalid name for the same square, explaining why each is valid or invalid.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (naming square), section 8.2 p.193
exercise.description: Identify which of the four given names (PQSR, SPQR, RSPQ, QRSP) is not a valid name for the given square.

items.prompt: State the two properties that every rectangle must satisfy. Then explain why a square is also a rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rectangle must have (R1) opposite sides equal and (R2) all four angles equal to 90°. A square satisfies both: its opposite sides are equal (in fact all four sides are equal) and all its angles are 90°, so every square is a rectangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two rectangle properties (R1, R2) and verify a square satisfies both.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the two rectangle properties stated in section 8.2 and check each one against a drawn square.
inclusivity.challenge: Describe a shape that satisfies R2 (all angles 90°) but not R1 (opposite sides equal) and explain why such a shape cannot be closed with four sides.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.2 p.194
exercise.description: Draw the rectangle-and-four-squares configuration on dot paper and describe what was done to place the four squares symmetrically around the rectangle.

items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 6 cm and BC = 3 cm, point X lies on AD and point Y lies on BC. Explain why XY is shortest when X is directly opposite Y (that is, when AX = BY).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When AX = BY, the segment XY is perpendicular to both AD and BC, making it the shortest path between the two parallel sides. Any other position tilts XY, creating a longer slanted path between the same two parallel lines; the perpendicular distance between parallel lines is the minimum distance.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that the perpendicular distance between two parallel lines is the minimum distance, so XY is shortest when it is perpendicular to both sides.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rectangle on paper, mark a few positions of X and Y, measure XY each time, and identify when it is smallest.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one side length and re-examine whether the same reasoning still holds; articulate the general principle in one sentence.

exercise.description: In rectangle ABCD (AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm), predict and verify by measurement: at which positions of X on AD and Y on BC are they closest and farthest apart?

items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD, the farthest apart that X (on AD) and Y (on BC) can be is the length of the diagonal. Explain why this is true using the properties of the rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The farthest positions place X at one end of AD (say at A) and Y at the opposite end of BC (say at C); the segment AC is then a diagonal of the rectangle. Because both X and Y are constrained to lie on the two opposite sides, the segment XY can never be longer than this diagonal, and it reaches that maximum exactly when X = A and Y = C (or X = D and Y = B).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that the maximum XY is achieved when X and Y are at diagonally opposite corners of the rectangle, making XY a diagonal.

inclusivity.support: Use a pair-share: one partner explains which positions they think give the maximum, and the other checks by measuring.
inclusivity.challenge: If the rectangle's dimensions change (longer or shorter sides), does the diagonal — and hence the maximum XY — increase or decrease? Formulate a general claim.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: Draw any rectangle PQRS and its two diagonals PR and QS. Measure the lengths of both diagonals. What do you notice? Now explain why you think this will always be true for any rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two diagonals PR and QS are equal in length. This holds because the rectangle has all right angles and equal opposite sides; each diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle formed by one pair of adjacent sides. Since both triangles share the same two side lengths, their hypotenuses — the diagonals — must also be equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fact that in a rectangle each diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs equal to the rectangle's two sides, so both diagonals are equal.

inclusivity.support: Measure both diagonals of at least two differently shaped rectangles and record in a table before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Alter one angle so the figure is no longer a rectangle (make it a parallelogram) and check whether the diagonals remain equal; use the result to refine your explanation.

exercise.book_ref: Explore (diagonal bisects angles equally), section 8.5 p.204
exercise.description: Determine how the rectangle must be constructed so that its diagonal divides the opposite angles into two equal parts.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: A diagonal of a rectangle divides the right angle at each corner into two smaller angles. If the diagonal divides one corner into 35° and 55°, what are the two angles at the opposite corner? Justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two angles at the opposite corner are also 35° and 55°. The diagonal creates two triangles inside the rectangle; the angles at opposite corners are corresponding angles in congruent triangles (the triangles share the diagonal and have equal sides from the rectangle's properties), so the angle split at one corner is mirrored at the opposite corner.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the symmetry of the two right triangles formed by the diagonal: equal opposite sides mean equal angle pairs at opposite corners.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rectangle, mark the 35° and 55° angles at one corner, then measure the angles at the opposite corner to check before writing the justification.
inclusivity.challenge: What if the diagonal divides one corner into 45° and 45°? What does this tell you about the rectangle's sides? Explain.

exercise.description: Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: A rectangle has one side of length 5 cm and a diagonal of length 13 cm. A student claims the other side must be 12 cm. Using the right-triangle relationship formed by a side, the adjacent side, and the diagonal, verify whether the student's claim is correct. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the two sides of the rectangle. So the other side = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. The student's claim is correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the right-triangle relationship: (other side)² = (diagonal)² − (known side)² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the other side = 12 cm.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rectangle and its diagonal, label the known side (5 cm) and diagonal (13 cm), and identify the right triangle before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a different pair of whole-number side lengths whose diagonal is also a whole number, and construct that rectangle.

exercise.description: Construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm.

items.prompt: When X on side AD and Y on side BC of rectangle ABCD satisfy AX = BY, the quadrilateral ABYX is a rectangle. Give two reasons — one about side lengths and one about angles — to support this claim.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Side reason: AB and XY are both perpendicular to AD and BC; since AD and BC are parallel and AX = BY, XY = AB, so the opposite sides AB and XY are equal (and AX = BY by construction), satisfying R1. Angle reason: since ABCD is a rectangle, angle A = 90°; and since AX is part of AD (a side of the rectangle), angle XAB = 90°; similarly angle YBA = 90° and, by the rectangle property, angle BYX = 90°, confirming all angles are 90°, satisfying R2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90°) applied to the sub-quadrilateral ABYX, justified by the rectangle's own properties.

inclusivity.support: Draw rectangle ABCD, mark X and Y with AX = BY = 2 cm, and measure the sides and angles of ABYX before writing the two reasons.
inclusivity.challenge: What happens to the shape of ABYX if AX ≠ BY? Is it still a rectangle? Explain using the same two criteria.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: A classmate says: 'If a rectangle's diagonal divides its corner angle into two equal halves, the rectangle must be a square.' Do you agree? Explain using what you know about angles and sides of rectangles and squares.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the claim is correct. In a rectangle the corner angle is 90°. If the diagonal bisects it, each half is 45°. For the diagonal to make a 45° angle with a side, the two sides forming that corner must be equal (since tan 45° = 1 implies the two legs of the right triangle are equal). Equal adjacent sides in a rectangle means all four sides are equal, which is the defining property of a square. So the rectangle must be a square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that a 45°–45° diagonal bisection implies equal adjacent sides, which means the rectangle is a square.

inclusivity.support: Construct one rectangle where the diagonal divides the corner into 45° and 45°, measure both sides, and report what you find before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Alter the premise: what if the diagonal divides the corner into 30° and 60°? What can you say about the ratio of the two sides? Explain.

exercise.description: Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold.

items.prompt: A wavy wave is to be drawn on a baseline of 12 cm, with each complete wave occupying an equal portion of the baseline. What radius should be set on the compass to draw each half-circle? What is the length AX for the first wave?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each complete wave occupies 3 cm of the baseline (12 cm ÷ 4 waves = 3 cm per wave). Each half-circle has a diameter equal to one wave's width (3 cm), so the radius is 1.5 cm. AX = 3 cm (the width of the first wave's base).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the baseline equally among the number of waves to find each wave's width; the radius is half that width, and AX equals that width.

inclusivity.support: Draw the 12 cm baseline, mark it into equal sections for each wave, then identify the diameter of each half-circle before computing the radius.
inclusivity.challenge: If the baseline is 15 cm and the waves must be identical, how many waves fit and what radius is needed? What if the waves need not be identical in width?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191
exercise.description: What radius should be taken in the compass to draw the first half-circle of the Wavy Wave? What should be the length of AX?

items.prompt: A student wants to draw a wavy wave on a baseline of 20 cm using half-circles of radius 2.5 cm. How many complete half-circles will fit on the baseline? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each half-circle has diameter = 2 × 2.5 = 5 cm, so it occupies 5 cm of the baseline. Number of half-circles = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 complete half-circles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the diameter of each half-circle (2 × radius), then divide the baseline length by the diameter to find the count.

inclusivity.support: Mark off 5 cm segments on a 20 cm line to count how many fit, then connect this to the calculation.
inclusivity.challenge: If the baseline were 22 cm with the same radius, could the student fit complete half-circles end-to-end? What adjustment would make it work?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191
exercise.description: Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave on it.

items.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would construct a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm using only a ruler and compass. State which property you are ensuring at each step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Draw side AB = 6 cm (one long side). Step 2: At A, use compass arcs to raise a perpendicular — this ensures the angle at A is 90° (R2). Step 3: Mark D on the perpendicular at AD = 4 cm (one short side). Step 4: At B, raise a perpendicular in the same manner (R2 at B). Step 5: Open the compass to 4 cm and, from B, mark C on the perpendicular at BC = 4 cm (R1: BC = AD). Step 6: Join DC; measure DC to verify DC = AB = 6 cm (R1 confirmed).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply R2 (90° angles) at each base corner by raising perpendiculars, then apply R1 (equal opposite sides) by using the compass to transfer the side length.

inclusivity.support: Carry out the construction with compass and ruler first, then write the steps by describing what you actually did.
inclusivity.challenge: Could you construct the same rectangle starting from the short side (4 cm) first? Write the steps and compare the two methods.

exercise.description: Draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

items.prompt: A student draws a 4-sided figure in which all four angles are 90°. What can you conclude about the figure?

options.label: A
options.text: It could be any quadrilateral because the angle condition alone does not constrain the sides.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be a rectangle because opposite sides must be equal when all angles are 90°.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be a square because all angles are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: It must have all sides equal because right angles force equal sides.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The figure must be a rectangle. When all four angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, the angle sum is 360° (consistent), and the geometric constraint forces opposite sides to be equal — it is impossible to close the figure otherwise. It need not be a square unless all sides are also equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the geometric result that a quadrilateral with all four angles equal to 90° must have equal opposite sides (rectangle property R1), making it a rectangle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the angle property of squares with rectangles; all angles being 90° identifies a rectangle, not necessarily a square.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not recognise that four right angles geometrically force equal opposite sides; the side constraint is not independent of the angle constraint.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-applies the constraint; right angles force opposite sides to be equal, not all sides to be equal — that additional condition would make it a square.

inclusivity.support: Try to draw a 4-sided figure with all right angles where opposite sides are not equal; notice that the figure cannot close.
inclusivity.challenge: What additional condition would you need to impose on the rectangle to make it a square? Write it as a property statement.

exercise.description: Draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

items.prompt: Using the compass length-transfer technique, construct a rectangle that can be divided into exactly three identical squares, where the side of each square is 3 cm. What are the dimensions of the rectangle? Show the transfer steps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each square has side 3 cm. Three squares placed side by side give a rectangle of length 9 cm and breadth 3 cm. Construction: set one side AF = 3 cm; use the compass to transfer AF three times along the long side, marking B at 3 cm, then a second transfer to 6 cm, then a third to 9 cm; raise a perpendicular at 9 cm; mark the height at 3 cm; complete the rectangle. Dimensions: 9 cm × 3 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Transfer the square-side length three times using the compass along the long direction, then raise a perpendicular and complete the rectangle at height equal to the square side.

inclusivity.support: Draw three squares of side 3 cm on dot paper first to see the target shape, then use the compass to reproduce it on plain paper without the dots.
inclusivity.challenge: What is the smallest rectangle that can be divided into both two identical squares AND three identical squares simultaneously? Explain your reasoning.

exercise.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares.

items.prompt: A rectangle has sides 8 cm and 4 cm. Describe how you would find the centre of this rectangle and use it to draw a square inside the rectangle with the square's centre coinciding with the rectangle's centre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw both diagonals of the rectangle; they intersect at the rectangle's centre. The largest square that fits inside the rectangle has side equal to the shorter side of the rectangle (4 cm). Mark the four corners of the inner square by measuring 2 cm from the centre along the direction of each side of the rectangle, then connect these four points. Verify that the inner square has all sides 4 cm and all angles 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate the centre by intersecting the diagonals, then construct the inscribed square (side = shorter rectangle side) by measuring equal distances from the centre along each axis.

inclusivity.support: Construct the 8 cm × 4 cm rectangle and physically draw both diagonals to find the centre point before attempting the inner square.
inclusivity.challenge: What is the largest square whose centre coincides with the rectangle's centre but whose corners lie on the rectangle's sides (not just inside)? Find its side length and describe the construction.

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it such that the centre of the square coincides with the centre of the rectangle.

items.prompt: In the Shadings construction challenge, a student wants to draw a square of side 6 cm containing a smaller square of side 2 cm at its centre, with a uniform gap between the two squares. What is the width of the gap on each side? Describe how you would locate the corners of the inner square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The outer square has side 6 cm and the inner square has side 2 cm. The total gap on one axis is 6 − 2 = 4 cm, shared equally on both sides, so the gap on each side is 2 cm. Locate the centre of the outer square by intersecting its diagonals; then measure 1 cm from the centre towards each side (half of 2 cm) to mark the corners of the inner square, or equivalently measure 2 cm inward from each side of the outer square along the perpendicular bisector of each side.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the gap as (outer side − inner side) ÷ 2; locate the inner square's corners by measuring that gap inward from each side of the outer square.

inclusivity.support: Draw the 6 cm square on dot paper and mark the inner 2 cm square by counting dot-units inward from each side before transferring the construction to plain paper.
inclusivity.challenge: Design a three-layer nesting (outer, middle, inner square) in which each gap is the same width; choose dimensions and describe the construction.

exercise.description: Construct a shading figure (a square containing smaller squares) with measurements of own choice.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: Two points B and C are 6 cm apart. You want to find a point A that is exactly 5 cm from both B and C. Describe the arc-intersection method and state how many such points A exist.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw segment BC = 6 cm. Set the compass to 5 cm. Draw an arc of radius 5 cm centred at B (all points 5 cm from B). Draw a second arc of radius 5 cm centred at C. The two arcs intersect at two points, one above and one below BC. Either intersection point is a valid apex A, exactly 5 cm from both B and C. So there are two such points A.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw arcs of radius 5 cm centred at each of B and C; the two intersection points are the two points equidistant (5 cm) from both B and C.

inclusivity.support: Draw segment BC and the two full circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and C first, then identify the intersection points before switching to arcs.
inclusivity.challenge: If the required distance were 2 cm instead of 5 cm (while BC remains 6 cm), would the two arcs still intersect? Explain why or why not.

exercise.description: Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: Using the arc-intersection technique from the House construction, explain how you would construct a rhombus (a 4-sided figure with all sides equal but not a square) with all sides 5 cm and one diagonal of 6 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw the diagonal AC = 6 cm. To find vertex B: set the compass to 5 cm, draw an arc from A and an arc from C; their intersection above AC gives B (equidistant 5 cm from both A and C). To find vertex D: draw the same arcs below AC; the intersection gives D. Join AB, BC, CD, DA to complete the rhombus ABCD. All four sides are 5 cm (enforced by the equal-radius arcs), but the angles at A and C differ from 90° (they are acute), confirming it is not a square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use arc-intersection with radius 5 cm from both ends of the 6 cm diagonal to locate the two off-diagonal vertices, then join all four to form the rhombus.

inclusivity.support: Begin by drawing the diagonal AC = 6 cm and marking it; then recall how the House apex was found from two base corners using equal arcs, and apply the same idea here.
inclusivity.challenge: Construct the same rhombus and then measure all four angles; identify which angles are equal and explain why using the symmetry of the construction.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: To construct a point A that is the same distance from point B as it is from point C, which of the following correctly describes the arc-intersection method?

options.label: A
options.text: Draw a circle centred at the midpoint of BC; A is any point on this circle.

options.label: B
options.text: Draw a perpendicular to BC at its midpoint; A is the midpoint itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Draw arcs of different radii from B and from C; A is where they cross.

options.label: D
options.text: Draw arcs of the same radius from B and from C; A is one of the points where the two arcs meet.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw arcs of the same radius from B and from C; A is one of the points where the two arcs meet. Both arcs have the same radius, so every point on arc B is the same distance from B, and every point on arc C is the same distance from C; the intersection satisfies both conditions simultaneously.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Equal-radius arcs from each given point intersect at the points equidistant from both; the radius chosen equals the required distance.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the equidistant-from-two-points locus (a perpendicular bisector) with a circle centred at the midpoint; these are different sets of points.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies the midpoint of BC, which is equidistant from B and C, but does not recognise that the arc-intersection method finds any point at a specified equal distance, not just the midpoint.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Using arcs of different radii would place A at different distances from B and C, which violates the equidistant requirement.

inclusivity.support: Re-read the House construction in section 8.6 and identify which step sets the equal radius, then match it to the option choices.
inclusivity.challenge: If you use arcs of radius r from B and C, and BC = d, what is the condition on r relative to d for the arcs to intersect? Explain geometrically.

exercise.description: Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm.
